claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has previously been produced in a hierarchical-heterostructured state.

A hybrid model combining imaging-derived microstructural descriptors, CALPHAD inputs, and machine learning can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness for hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
The hybrid model will compute predictions faster than full-scale atomistic and conventional machine-learning simulations.
The hybrid model will be more accurate than full-scale atomistic and conventional machine-learning simulations.
High-resolution imaging can provide descriptors representing the key hierarchical microstructural features of the alloy.
A minimal set of CALPHAD-derived thermophysical parameters provides decisive information for the mechanical-property model.
Using imaging descriptors and reduced CALPHAD inputs bypasses the need for exhaustive first-principles and full-scale simulations.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations mediate local stress distributions in hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical microstructural features mediate deformation mechanisms in HfNbTiVAl10.
Imaging-derived descriptors capture the stress-distribution and deformation effects of the multilevel heterogeneities.
Spatial microstructural fluctuations largely govern the alloy’s Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
Quantifying structural heterogeneities and combining them with thermophysical inputs reduces computational demand.
The model will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 50% relative to existing full-scale simulation methods.
The model will reduce computational costs by approximately one order of magnitude.
Faster property estimation will enable more rapid alloy-design iterations.
Full-scale first-principles, CALPHAD, and standard machine-learning approaches have high computational costs.
Full-scale first-principles, CALPHAD, and standard machine-learning approaches have lower predictive power for fracture behavior than the proposed model.
The approach may become unreliable when imaging does not resolve mechanically critical heterogeneities.
The approach may become unreliable when dynamic microstructural evolution dominates mechanical behavior.
The approach may become unreliable at extreme temperatures or strain rates because the learned microstructure-property correlations can change.
